byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: 166 million motor vehicles, nearly three in four Americans in towns and cities, and a baby born in 1984 could expect to live to 75.

items.title: Population
items.summary: The United States had about 236 to 239 million people in 1984.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Population, total
Our World in Data: Population (UN World Population Prospects, HYDE)

items.title: Life expectancy at birth
items.summary: A baby born in 1984 could expect to live about 74.6 years.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Life expectancy at birth, total (years)
Our World in Data: Life expectancy (UN World Population Prospects and other series)

items.title: Town and city
items.summary: About 74 percent of Americans lived in urban areas.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Urban population (% of total)

items.title: Infant deaths
items.summary: About 11 of every 1,000 babies died before their first birthday.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Mortality rate, infant (per 1,000 live births)

items.title: Births per woman
items.summary: The fertility rate was 1.81 births per woman.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Fertility rate, total (births per woman)

items.title: Motor vehicles
items.summary: Registrations reached 166.2 million: 128.2 million cars, 37.5 million trucks and 584,000 buses.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Df339-342: Motor vehicle registrations
FHWA Highway Statistics Summary to 1995, Table MV-200: Motor vehicle registrations

byTheNumbers.scarcityNote: Literacy and household size were not found for 1984. There was no census; population figures are mid-year estimates.

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen

items.title: The first Papa John's
items.summary: John Schnatter opened the first Papa John's Pizza in Jeffersonville, Indiana, on 2 October 1984.

foodAndKitchen.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1984 food prices, appliance counts or meals; the pages we opened on fast food had no 1984 figures.

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: Athletic wear went out on the street, shoulder pads went into jackets and Miami Vice put pastel jackets on men.

items.title: Leg warmers and tracksuits
items.summary: Athletic accessories such as leg warmers, wide belts and elastic headbands were a massive trend in the early 1980s, and ripped sweatshirts, tights and velour tracksuits were worn on the street.

items.title: The Madonna look
items.summary: Many of the clothes Madonna wore in 1983-85, including tube skirts, oversized tops and 'Boy Toy' belt buckles, were widely copied, and jelly bracelets were inspired by her in 1983.

items.title: Shoulder pads
items.summary: Shoulder pads became common among career-driven women, popularised by Dynasty, from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s.

items.title: Miami Vice
items.summary: Colourful men's styles, prompted by series such as Miami Vice, were an explosion of the mid-1980s, and Don Johnson's Ray-Ban Wayfarers lifted sales to 720,000 units in 1984.

items.title: Members Only
items.summary: New-wave influence, including Members Only jackets, shaped fashion from the early to mid-1980s, and women's fashion became more colourful around 1982.

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: A production worker in manufacturing earned about $374 a week.

items.title: A manufacturing paycheque
items.summary: A production worker in manufacturing earned $9.19 an hour, or $374.03 a week, on average; in durable goods $402.82 and in non-durable goods $333.08.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Ba4361-4366: Hourly and weekly earnings of production workers in manufacturing, 1909-1995

workAndWages.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced figures for 1984 hours, women's work or the minimum wage.

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced school-year, enrolment or toy figures for 1984: the NCES table we opened has an estimate only to 1979-80.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.standfirst: The first woman captain of a Boeing 747 took command in July.

items.title: A woman in command of a 747
items.summary: Beverly Burns became the first female Boeing 747 captain in the world on 18 July 1984.

gettingAround.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1984 fares or journey times; the vehicle count is under The year in numbers.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.standfirst: The Bell System was broken up on New Year's Day.

items.title: The Bell System breaks up
items.summary: The U.S. Bell System was broken up on 1 January 1984.

keepingInTouch.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1984 postage rates or telephone and modem counts.

healthAndMedicine.title: Health and medicine
healthAndMedicine.standfirst: The virus that causes AIDS was named in April.

items.title: The cause of AIDS
items.summary: On 23 April 1984 Health Secretary Margaret Heckler announced that the virus HTLV-III was the cause of AIDS.

sensitivity.note: This item concerns a disease that caused many deaths.

items.title: A first embryo transfer
items.summary: Dr John Buster's team announced the first embryo transfer from one woman to another that resulted in a live birth, on 3 February 1984.

healthAndMedicine.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1984 doctor fees, hospital costs or vaccination figures.

leisureAndFun.title: Evenings, weekends and festivals
leisureAndFun.standfirst: Workouts, headphones and rented videotapes, with summer blockbusters and an Olympics in Los Angeles.

items.title: The aerobics boom
items.summary: Jane Fonda's Workout video of 1982 helped spread aerobics worldwide and sparked an industry boom; aerobic dancing dated from Jacki Sorensen in 1969 and Kenneth Cooper's book Aerobics of 1968.

items.title: The Walkman
items.summary: Sony's Walkman reached the United States in June 1980; cassettes outsold vinyl for the first time in 1983 and over 100 million Walkmans had been sold by 1989.

items.title: Renting a tape
items.summary: By mid-1985 the United States had 15,000 video rental stores; the first professionally managed one, Video Station, opened in Los Angeles in December 1977.

items.title: A summer at the cinema
items.summary: Ghostbusters and Gremlins were released on 8 June 1984, The Karate Kid on 22 June and Purple Rain on 25 June.

items.title: The Los Angeles Olympics
items.summary: The Summer Olympics were held in Los Angeles from 28 July to 12 August 1984, after the Soviet Union announced a boycott on 8 May.

items.title: New on television
items.summary: Jeopardy! began its syndicated run on 10 September, Miami Vice premiered on NBC on 16 September, The Transformers debuted on 17 September and American Movie Classics launched on 1 October 1984.

spotlight.title: Computers come home
spotlight.standfirst: On 24 January 1984 Apple put a $2,495 computer with a mouse on sale after a Super Bowl advertisement, in a year when fewer than one in ten homes had a computer.

items.title: The Macintosh
items.summary: The Macintosh went on sale on 24 January 1984 for $2,495, with 128 KB of memory, a built-in 9-inch screen of 512 by 342 pixels and a single 400 KB floppy drive.
items.metric: Price of the Macintosh at launch

items.title: The '1984' advertisement
items.summary: Apple's '1984' commercial, directed by Ridley Scott at a cost of $1.5 million, ran during the third quarter of Super Bowl XVIII on 22 January 1984.

items.title: Seventy thousand
items.summary: The Macintosh reached 70,000 units on 3 May 1984, a hundred days after launch.

items.title: Few homes had one
items.summary: By 1982 about 621,000 American households had a home computer at an average price of $530, and in 1987 only 15 percent of homes had one; the Commodore 64 was among the most popular.

items.title: The IBM PC
items.summary: IBM introduced its Personal Computer in August 1981, and the PCjr followed in 1983 or early 1984 (the article gives both dates).
